analysis.one_liner: Pauses new petrochemical plant permits, imposes stricter pollution rules on plastics production, and cuts single-use plastics.
analysis.headline: Introduced with five weeks left in the Congress and only two cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it arrived and never received a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have forced a major overhaul of how plastics are made in the United States. It would have paused new federal permits for petrochemical and plastics plants until the EPA finished stricter air and water rules, required pollution monitoring right at the fence lines of those plants, and given nearby communities a formal say and a community benefit agreement before any new permit. It would also have set national targets to cut single-use plastic packaging by at least 25% and shift at least 30% of plastic packaging to reusable or refillable systems by 2032, and funded studies of microplastics in food and in the human body.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near plastics and petrochemical facilities, who the bill's findings describe as disproportionately low-income communities and communities of color exposed to cancer- and birth-defect-linked pollutants, would gain real-time air monitoring, a say in permits, and a pause on new plants. Consumers would gain reduced single-use plastic packaging and better information on microplastics in food and in the human body.

how_it_helps.text: During a 'temporary pause period' the EPA could not issue new Clean Air Act or Clean Water Act permits for petrochemical and plastics facilities, and the export of covered plastic products was prohibited, until new air and water rules were in effect.

The bill requires an environmental justice assessment, notification in residents' own languages, a public hearing in the community with at least 60 days' notice, and a community benefit agreement before a covered facility permit can be approved.

It requires continuous fenceline air monitoring around covered facilities, with the data made available to the public in real time, and tighter emission standards for flaring, equipment leaks, and storage vessels.
It sets federal targets to reduce single-use plastic packaging and food service ware by at least 25% by 2032 and to shift at least 30% of plastic packaging to reuse and refill by 2032.

It directs a nationwide FDA study of microplastics in food and NIH research on microplastics in the human body, and creates a grant program for refillable and reusable packaging projects, with priority for low-income communities and communities of color.
It requires EPA to begin a rulemaking to list discarded polyvinyl chloride (PVC) as a hazardous waste and to prioritize styrene and vinyl chloride for toxic-substance review.

analysis.who_pays: Plastics and petrochemical producers would bear the cost: the permit pause, stricter air and water standards, continuous fenceline monitoring, community benefit agreements, and a siting ban would all fall on facilities that make plastic resins and chemicals. Those costs, along with delayed plant construction, could raise packaging and goods prices for consumers.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have blocked new permits for plastics and petrochemical facilities and banned new or expanded facilities within five miles of any school, residence, hospital, park, or community center — restrictions an honest supporter would acknowledge could halt plant construction and the jobs that come with it in industrial regions.

It sets zero-discharge effluent limits for priority pollutants and plastic pellets unless the EPA formally justifies higher limits, and requires sweeping air, water, and toxic-substance rulemakings on one-to-three-year deadlines, a compliance burden concentrated on one industry that could raise costs passed to consumers in packaging and goods prices.

Because the bill was written to amend the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, and toxic-substance law all at once, its broad new definitions — covering everything from nurdles to waste-to-fuel incinerators — would give the EPA wide discretionary power over a major manufacturing sector with limited opportunity for challenge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and concentrated on a specific group: the bill's own findings state that plastics facilities are more likely to be sited in low-income communities and communities of color, exposing them to pollutants linked to cancer and birth defects, and the bill attacks that directly with monitoring, community consent, and a building pause. The costs fall on the petrochemical and plastics industry and would partly show up as higher packaging prices and forgone plant construction. The design is aggressive — near-zero discharge limits, a five-mile siting ban, and simultaneous overhauls of three environmental statutes on tight deadlines — which is the kind of ambition that invites the fair criticism that it was more a statement of demands than a negotiable bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate in the last month of the Congress, referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, and died there without ever getting a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the bill on December 1, 2022, the final month of the 117th Congress, which ended on January 3, 2023.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
No further action ever occurred: the committee held no markup, and the bill never received a floor vote in either chamber.

The bill's findings stated that plastics production is projected to double within a decade and that petrochemical facilities are more likely to be located in low-income communities and communities of color.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Plastics and petrochemical producers are better off because the bill died: no permit pause, stricter emissions rules, fenceline monitoring, or siting restrictions took effect, and planned plant expansions faced no new federal obstacles. Businesses that depend on low-cost single-use plastic packaging also avoided the bill's reduction and reuse targets.

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would pause new petrochemical permits, tighten air and water rules for plastics facilities, and require environmental justice reviews.

against.name: Tom Carper
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill shows no committee action after its referral on the day it was introduced.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; the only senators involved, sponsor Cory Booker and cosponsors Jeff Merkley and Chris Van Hollen, were all Democrats, so the record shows no partisan split.

industries.note: The bill's core provisions — a permit moratorium, stricter air and water standards, mandatory fenceline monitoring, community benefit agreements, and a ban on new facilities within five miles of schools and homes — all fall directly on companies that make ethylene, propylene, and plastic resins. Its findings describe these facilities as disproportionate pollution sources for nearby low-income communities and communities of color.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies supplying petrochemical feedstocks
industries.note: Because the bill projects plastics as the largest future driver of oil and gas demand, restricting plastics production would shrink a growth market for these companies. Their interest in continued plastics expansion runs against the bill's public health goals.

industries.industry: Single-use packaging and consumer goods companies
industries.note: The bill requires a 25% cut in single-use plastic packaging and food service ware by 2032 and 30% reuse and refill targets, forcing changes to packaging across food, beverage, and consumer products. Medical devices, hygiene products, and hazardous-material shipping are excluded.

The bill treats pyrolysis, gasification, and waste-to-fuel facilities as covered polluting facilities rather than as recycling, bars them from the National Recycling Strategy, and would list discarded PVC as hazardous waste. Its findings call these technologies 'not a sustainable solution.'

The bill creates a competitive grant program for reuse and refill projects, with priority for projects benefiting low-income communities and communities of color, and sets mandatory refill targets that would create demand for these systems.
